Africa
Africa is the world's second-largest and second-most populous <color=#3366CC>continent</color> after <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. At about 30.3 million km2 (11.7
million square miles) including adjacent islands, it covers around 20% of <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>'s land area and 6% of its total surface
area. With nearly billion of the <color=#3366CC>world population</color>, Africa's population is the youngest among the continents; the median
age in 2012 was 19.7, when the worldwide median age was 30.4. Based on 2024 projections, Africa's population will
exceed 3.8 billion people by 2100. Africa is the least wealthy inhabited continent per capita and second-least wealthy
by total wealth, ahead of <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>. Scholars have attributed this to various factors including <color=#3366CC>geography</color>, climate,
corruption, <color=#3366CC>colonialism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, and <color=#3366CC>neocolonialism</color>. Despite this low concentration of wealth, the African
economy is home to many of the world's fastest-growing economies.
Africa straddles the <color=#3366CC>equator</color> and the <color=#3366CC>prime meridian</color>. The continent is surrounded by the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color> to the

north, the <color=#3366CC>Arabian plate</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Aqaba</color> to the northeast, the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color> to the southeast and the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic</color>

<color=#3366CC>Ocean</color> to the west. <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Yemen</color> have parts of their territories located on African
geographical soil, mostly in the form of islands.
The continent includes <color=#3366CC>Madagascar</color> and various archipelagos. It contains 54 fully recognised sovereign states, eight
cities and islands that are part of non-African states, and two de facto independent states with limited or no recognition.
This count does not include <color=#3366CC>Malta</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>, which are geologically part of the African continent. <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> is the largest
country by area, and <color=#3366CC>Nigeria</color> is largest by population. Nations cooperate through the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>African</color>
<color=#3366CC>Union</color>, which is headquartered in <color=#3366CC>Addis Ababa</color>.
Africa is highly biodiverse; it is the continent with the largest number of <color=#3366CC>megafauna</color> species, as it was least affected by
the <color=#3366CC>extinction of the Pleistocene megafauna</color>. However, its is heavily affected by a wide range of environmental issues,
including desertification, deforestation, water scarcity, and pollution. These entrenched environmental concerns are
expected to worsen as <color=#3366CC>climate change impacts Africa</color>. The UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has
identified Africa as the continent most <color=#3366CC>vulnerable to climate change</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>history of Africa</color> is long, complex, and varied, and has often been under-appreciated by the global historical
community. In African societies the oral word is revered, and they have generally recorded their history via oral
tradition, which has led anthropologists to term them "oral civilisations", contrasted with "literate civilisations" which
pride the written word. <color=#3366CC>African culture</color> is rich and diverse both within and across regions, encompassing <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>cuisine</color>,
<color=#3366CC>music</color> and dance, religion, and dress.
Africa, particularly <color=#3366CC>Eastern Africa</color>, is widely accepted to be the place of origin of humans and the <color=#3366CC>Hominidae</color> clade, also
known as the great apes. The earliest hominids and their ancestors have been dated to around 7 million years ago, and
<color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> (modern human) are believed to have originated in Africa 350,000 to 260,000 years ago. Throughout
history the continent saw the rise and fall of many kingdoms and empires, such as <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Makuria</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Fatimids</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mali</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Asante</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kongo</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Luba</color>, Bunyoro, <color=#3366CC>Great Zimbabwe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Imerina</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Zulu</color>. Despite the
predominance of states, many societies were heterarchical and <color=#3366CC>stateless</color>. <color=#3366CC>Slave trades</color> created various diasporas,
especially in the Americas. From the late-19th century to early 20th century, driven by the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color>,
most of Africa was <color=#3366CC>rapidly conquered and colonised</color> by European nations, save for <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Liberia</color>. European rule
had significant impacts on Africa's societies, and colonies were maintained for the purpose of economic exploitation
and extraction of natural resources. Most present states emerged from <color=#3366CC>a process of decolonisation</color> following <color=#3366CC>World War</color>
<color=#3366CC>II</color> and established the <color=#3366CC>Organisation of African Unity</color> in 1963, the predecessor to the African Union. The nascent
countries decided to keep their colonial borders, with traditional power structures used in governance to varying
degrees.
Etymology
Afri was a Latin name used to refer to the inhabitants of what was then known as northern Africa, located west of the
<color=#3366CC>Nile</color> river, and in its widest sense referring to all lands south of the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color>, also known as Ancient Libya. This
name seems to have originally referred to a native Libyan tribe, an ancestor of modern <color=#3366CC>Berbers</color>; see <color=#3366CC>Terence</color> for
discussion. The name had usually been connected with the Phoenician word afar meaning "dust", but a 1981
hypothesis has asserted that it stems from the <color=#3366CC>Berber</color> word ifri (plural ifran) meaning "cave", in reference to cave
dwellers. The same word may be found in the name of the Banu Ifran from <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tripolitania</color>, a Berber tribe
originally from Yafran (also known as Ifrane) in northwestern <color=#3366CC>Libya</color>, as well as Ifrane, <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color>.
Under <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> rule, <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color> became the capital of the province Africa Proconsularis, following the Roman victory over
the <color=#3366CC>Carthaginians</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Third Punic War</color> in 146 BC, which also included the coastal part of modern Libya. The Latin
suffix -ica can sometimes be used to denote a land (e.g., in Celtica from <color=#3366CC>Celtae</color>, as used by <color=#3366CC>Julius Caesar</color>). The
medieval Muslim region of Ifriqiya, following its conquest of the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine (Eastern Roman)</color> Empire's Exarchatus
Africae, preserved a form of the name. According to the Romans, Africa lies to the west of <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, while "Asia" was used
to refer to <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> and lands to the east. In his <color=#3366CC>Geographia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color> draws a definite line between the two continents

by, indicating <color=#3366CC>Alexandria</color> along the <color=#3366CC>prime meridian</color> and making the <color=#3366CC>Isthmus of Suez</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> the boundary
between Asia and Africa. As Europeans came to understand the real extent of the continent, the idea of "Africa"
expanded with their knowledge.
Other etymological hypotheses have been postulated:
• 1st-century Jewish historian <color=#3366CC>Flavius Josephus</color> (Ant. 1.15) asserted that it was named for Epher, grandson of
<color=#3366CC>Abraham</color> according to <color=#3366CC>Genesis</color> 25:4, whose descendants, he claimed, had invaded Libya.
• <color=#3366CC>Isidore of Seville</color> in his 7th-century Etymologiae XIV.5.2. suggests it comes from the Latin aprica, meaning "sunny".
• Massey, in 1881, stated it is derived from the Egyptian af-rui-ka, meaning "to turn toward the opening of the Ka".
The ka is the energetic double of every person, and the "opening of the Ka" refers to a womb or birthplace. Africa
would be, for the Egyptians, "the birthplace".
• Michèle Fruyt in 1976 proposed linking the Latin word with africus "south wind", which would be of Umbrian origin
and mean originally "rainy wind".
• Robert R. Stieglitz of Rutgers University in 1984 proposed: "The name Africa, derived from the Latin *Aphir-ic-a, is
cognate to Hebrew Ophir ['rich']."
• Ibn Khallikan and some other historians claim the name came from a <color=#3366CC>Himyarite</color> king called Afrikin ibn Kais ibn Saifi
("Afrikus son of Abraham") who subdued Ifriqiya.
• Arabic afrīqā (feminine noun) and ifrīqiyā, now usually pronounced afrīqiyā (feminine) 'Africa', from afara [' = ain,
not alif] 'to be dusty' from afar 'dust, powder' and afir 'dried, dried up by the sun, withered' and affara 'to dry in the
sun on hot sand' or 'to sprinkle with dust'.
• Possibly Phoenician faraqa in the sense of 'colony, separation'.
The terms "<color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>" and "<color=#3366CC>Sub-Saharan Africa</color>" have been subject to recent criticism from some scholars due to its
historical root in colonialist discourse which arbitrarily separated Africa into a white "northern" Africa and black
"southern" Africa, overlooking common genetic links and regional diversity across the continent.
History
In accordance with <color=#3366CC>African cosmology</color>, African historical consciousness viewed historical change and continuity, order
and purpose within the framework of man and his environment, the gods, and his ancestors, and he believed himself
part of a holistic spiritual entity. In African societies, the historical process is largely a communal one, with eyewitness
accounts, hearsay, reminiscences, and occasionally visions, dreams, and hallucinations crafted into narrative oral
traditions which are performed and transmitted through generations.
In oral traditions time is sometimes mythical and social, and ancestors were considered historical actors. Mind and
memory shapes traditions, as events are condensed over time and crystallise into clichés.Oral tradition can be or. It
speaks to people according to their understanding, unveiling itself in accordance with their aptitudes. In African
epistemology, the epistemic subject "experiences the epistemic object in a sensuous, emotive, intuitive, abstractive
understanding, rather than through abstraction alone, as is the case in Western epistemology" to arrive at a "complete
knowledge", and as such oral traditions, <color=#3366CC>music</color>, proverbs, and the like were used in the preservation and transmission
of knowledge.
Prehistory
Africa is considered by most <color=#3366CC>paleoanthropologists</color> to be the <color=#3366CC>oldest inhabited territory</color> on Earth, with the Human species
originating from the continent. During the mid-20th century, anthropologists discovered many fossils and evidence of
human occupation perhaps as early as seven million years ago ("Before Present"; BP). Fossil remains of several
species of early apelike humans thought to have evolved into modern humans, such as <color=#3366CC>Australopithecus afarensis</color>
<color=#3366CC>radiometrically dated</color> to approximately 3.9–3.0 million BP, <color=#3366CC>Paranthropus boisei</color> (c. 2.3–1.4 million BP) and <color=#3366CC>Homo</color>
<color=#3366CC>ergaster</color> (c. 1.9 million–600,000 BP) have been discovered.
After the evolution of <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> approximately 350,000 to 260,000 BP, the continent was mainly populated by
groups of <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>. These first modern humans left Africa and populated the rest of the globe during the <color=#3366CC>Out of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Africa II</color> migration dated to approximately 50,000 years BP, exiting either across <color=#3366CC>Bab-el-Mandeb</color> over the Red Sea, the
<color=#3366CC>Strait of Gibraltar</color>, or the Isthmus of Suez.
Other migrations of modern humans have been dated to that time, with evidence of early human settlement found in
<color=#3366CC>southern Africa</color>, Southeast Africa, <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color>. During the African humid period, estimated to have
been around 10,500 BP, the Sahara had again become a green fertile valley, and its populations returned from the
interior and coastal highlands, with rock art paintings depicting a fertile Sahara and large populations discovered in
<color=#3366CC>Tassili n'Ajjer</color> dating back perhaps 10 millennia. However, the warming and drying climate meant that by 5,000 BP, the
Sahara region was becoming increasingly dry and hostile. Around 3500 BC, due to a tilt in <color=#3366CC>Earth's orbit</color>, the Sahara
experienced a period of rapid desertification. The domestication of cattle preceded agriculture and seems to have
existed alongside hunter-gatherer cultures. It is speculated that by 6,000 BP, cattle were domesticated in North Africa.
In <color=#3366CC>West Africa</color>, a wet phase ushered in an expanding <color=#3366CC>rainforest</color> and wooded <color=#3366CC>savanna</color> from Senegal to Cameroon.
Between 9,000 and 5,000 BP, <color=#3366CC>Niger–Congo speakers</color> domesticated the <color=#3366CC>oil palm</color> and raffia palm. <color=#3366CC>Black-eyed peas</color> and
<color=#3366CC>voandzeia</color> (African groundnuts) were domesticated, followed by <color=#3366CC>okra</color> and <color=#3366CC>kola nuts</color>. Since most of the plants grew in
the forest, the Niger–Congo speakers invented polished stone axes for clearing forest. <color=#3366CC>Pygmies</color> are thought to have
inhabited <color=#3366CC>Central Africa</color> for many millennia, splitting into eastern and western groups around 5,000 BP. Over 150,000
BP, there was an early dispersal of <color=#3366CC>anatomically modern humans</color> to Southern Africa, equated with the modern-day
Khoisan who have preserved their traditional hunter-gatherer way of life.
4th millennium BC – 6th century AD
Northeast Africa
From 3500 BC, nomes (ruled by nomarchs) coalesced to form the kingdoms of Lower Egypt and Upper Egypt in
northeast Africa. Around 3100 BC Upper Egypt conquered Lower Egypt to unify <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> under the 1st dynasty, with the
process of consolidation and assimilation completed by the time of the 3rd dynasty who formed the <color=#3366CC>Old Kingdom of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> in 2686 BC. The Kingdom of Kerma emerged around this time to become the dominant force in <color=#3366CC>Nubia</color>, controlling
territory as large as Egypt between the first and fourth cataracts of the Nile.
The height of the Old Kingdom saw the construction of many great pyramids, though under the 6th dynasty power
gradually decentralised to the nomarchs, culminating in the <color=#3366CC>disintegration of the kingdom</color>, exacerbated by drought and
famine. Around 2055 BC, the 11th dynasty, based in <color=#3366CC>Thebes</color>, conquered the others to form the <color=#3366CC>Middle Kingdom of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, and the 12th dynasty expanded into Lower Nubia at the expense of Kerma. Around 1700 BC, the Middle
Kingdom <color=#3366CC>fractured in two</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Hyksos</color> (a militaristic people from <color=#3366CC>Palestine</color>) invaded and conquered Lower Egypt,
while Kerma coordinated invasions deep into Egypt to reach its greatest extent. In 1550 BC, the 18th dynasty expelled
the Hyksos, and established the <color=#3366CC>New Kingdom of Egypt</color>. The New Kingdom conquered the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color> from the

<color=#3366CC>Canaanites</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mittani</color>, <color=#3366CC>Amorites</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Hittites</color>, and extinguished Kerma, incorporating Nubia into the empire, and sending
the Egyptian empire into its golden age. Internal struggles, drought, famine, and invasions by a <color=#3366CC>confederation of</color>
<color=#3366CC>seafaring peoples</color> contributed to the New Kingdom's <color=#3366CC>collapse in 1069 BC</color>.
The New Kingdom's collapse liberated the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kush</color> in Nubia, which manoeuvred into power in Upper Egypt
and conquered Lower Egypt in 754 BC to form the Kushite Empire. The Kushites ruled for a century and oversaw a
revival in pyramid building, until they were driven out of Egypt by the Assyrians in 663 BC in reprisal for their expansion
towards the <color=#3366CC>Assyrian Empire</color>. The Assyriansinstalled a puppet dynasty that later gained independence and once more
<color=#3366CC>unified Egypt</color>, until it was conquered by the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color> in 525 BC.
Egypt briefly regained independence from the Achaemenids under the 28th dynasty from 404 to 343 BC. The conquest
of Achaemenid Egypt by <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> in 332 BC marked the beginning of <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic rule</color> and the installation of
the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty. The Ptolemaics lost their holdings outside of Africa to the Seleucids in the <color=#3366CC>Syrian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wars</color>, expanded into <color=#3366CC>Cyrenaica</color>, and briefly occupied part of Kush in the 3rd century BC. In the 1st century BC,
Ptolemaic Egypt became entangled in a <color=#3366CC>Roman civil war</color>, leading to its conquest by the <color=#3366CC>Romans</color> in 30 BC. Kush
persisted as a major regional power until, having been weakened from internal rebellion amid worsening climatic
conditions, invasions by <color=#3366CC>Aksum</color> and the Noba caused their disintegration into <color=#3366CC>Makuria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alodia</color>, and Nobatia around the
5th century AD.
Horn of Africa
In the <color=#3366CC>Horn of Africa</color>, there was the <color=#3366CC>Land of Punt</color>, a kingdom on the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> which was a close trading partner of
Ancient Egypt in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC. Archaeologist Rodolfo Fattovich equates it to the Gash Group in the
Sudanese-Eritrean lowlands, and some scholars have hypothesised modern-day <color=#3366CC>Somalia</color>, while Kenneth Kitchen and
Felix Chami locate it on Zanzibar Island. In the Eritrean-<color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Highlands</color>, the kingdom of dmt rose c. 980 BC as the
region was incorporated into global trading networks, and it exhibited <color=#3366CC>Sabaean</color> influences which most scholars attribute
to a small migration of Sabaeans and their assimilation. Several scholars consider there to have been other
contemporaneous states, and dmt's collapse in the mid-1st century BC saw the region inhabited by small polities.
Modern-day Somalia was inhabited by nomadic pastoralists, and along the Horn's coast there were many ancient
Somali city-states that thrived off of the wider Red Sea trade and enjoyed a lucrative monopoly on cinnamon from India
due to their freedom from Roman interference. In the 1st century AD, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Aksum</color> rose from a city-state to
rule much of the northern Ethiopian-Eritrean Highlands and the Red Sea port of Adulis. Aksum was described as one of
the four great powers by Persian prophet <color=#3366CC>Mani</color> in the 3rd century. King <color=#3366CC>Ezana of Axum</color> converted from <color=#3366CC>traditional</color>
<color=#3366CC>religion</color> to <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> in the 4th century, gradually followed by the population. In the 6th century, Aksum conquered
South Arabia, though struggled to maintain control over it, and began to gradually lose its dominance over Red Sea
trade to Persians and Arabs.
Northwest Africa
Northwest Africa (the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color>) was inhabited by <color=#3366CC>Berber</color> semi-nomadic pastoralists. In the 1st millennium BC,
Phoenician migration and settlement came in search for precious metals in the Gulf of Tunis. This grew into <color=#3366CC>Ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Carthage</color> after gaining independence from <color=#3366CC>Phoenicia</color> in the 6th century BC, and they built an <color=#3366CC>extensive trading empire</color>
with a strict mercantile network. Carthage's collapse and conquest by Rome in the <color=#3366CC>Punic Wars</color> (3rd and 2nd centuries
BC) saw <color=#3366CC>Numidia</color> and Mauretania become major powers in the Maghreb.
Towards the end of the 2nd century BC Mauretania fought alongside King <color=#3366CC>Jugurtha</color> of Numidia against the Romans in
the Jugurthine War after he had usurped the Numidian throne from a Roman ally. Together they inflicted heavy
casualties, with the war ending inconclusively when King Bocchus I of Mauretania sold out Jugurtha to the Romans.
Around the turn of the millennium, both came under direct Roman rule. While Berber traditional religion predominated,
some converted to Christianity. In the 5th century AD the Vandals conquered Roman Africa before the <color=#3366CC>fall of Rome</color>,
though the province was reconquered by the <color=#3366CC>Byzantines</color> in the Vandalic War. Large swaths of indigenous peoples
regained self-governance in Masuna and its numerous successor polities in the Maghreb, including the kingdoms of
Ouarsenis, Aurès, and Altava.
West Africa
In the western <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color> the rise of settled communities occurred largely as a result of the domestication of <color=#3366CC>millet</color> and of
<color=#3366CC>sorghum</color>, and cattle <color=#3366CC>pastoralism</color> began c. 2500 BC. Extensive east-west belts of deserts, grasslands, and forests from
north to south were crucial for the moulding of their respective societies and meant that symbiotic trade relations
developed in response to the differing environments. Beginning around 4000 BC, the Tichitt culture in modern-day
Mauritania and Mali is the oldest known complexly organised society in West Africa, while others included the Kintampo
culture in modern-day Ghana, the <color=#3366CC>Nok culture</color> in modern-day Nigeria, and the Daima culture around <color=#3366CC>Lake Chad</color>.
Towards the end of the 3rd century AD, a <color=#3366CC>wet period</color> in the Sahel created areas for human habitation and exploitation
that had not been habitable for the best part of a millennium. The <color=#3366CC>Ghana Empire</color> (also called Wagadu) rose out of the
Tichitt culture, growing wealthy following the introduction of the camel to the western Sahel, which revolutionised the
<color=#3366CC>trans-Saharan trade</color> that linked their capital and Aoudaghost with Tahert and <color=#3366CC>Sijilmasa</color> in North Africa. Soninke tradition
holds that the final founding of Wagadu occurred after Dinga did a deal with Bida, a serpent deity who was guarding a
well, to sacrifice one maiden a year in exchange for assurance regarding plenty of rainfall and gold supply. Based on
<color=#3366CC>large tumuli</color> scattered across West Africa dating to this period, several scholars have speculated that there were further
simultaneous and preceding states relative to Wagadu.
Central, Eastern, and Southern Africa
In the grasslands of Cameroon, <color=#3366CC>Bantu</color>-speaking agriculturalists <color=#3366CC>migrated southward</color> sometime between 5000 BC and
3000 BC. Despite intensive research, the cause of the migrations, and that of the directions taken, is still unclear,
however there is consensus that there were multiple dispersal events. Around 1500 BC, Bantu speakers reached
central Cameroon. The 'Western Stream' likely followed the coast and the major rivers of the <color=#3366CC>Congo</color> system southwards
to reach the southern fringe of the <color=#3366CC>Congolian Rainforest</color> around 500 BC (some may have used the sea to circumvent
the rainforest). Their arrival coincided with the spread of iron metallurgy through Central Africa.
Meanwhile, the 'Eastern Stream' travelled either the northern fringe of the rainforest or the <color=#3366CC>Ubangi River</color> eastwards, and
reached just west of <color=#3366CC>Lake Victoria</color> around 500 BC. While there, Bantu speakers adopted iron metallurgy from Cushitic
speakers already present, and coexisted with them. Dispersal from the <color=#3366CC>Great Lakes region</color> occurred in two more
streams. One went west to meet the Western Stream in the DR Congo and Angola, while the other went south and
spread across Eastern and Southern Africa.
Around the turn of the millennium, Bantu speakers reached central modern-day Tanzania and near <color=#3366CC>Dar es Salaam</color>,
before rapidly moving southwards along the coast to reach modern-day <color=#3366CC>Kwazulu Natal</color> in South Africa around the 3rd
century AD. Throughout this, Bantu speakers displaced, replaced, or intermarried with and absorbed hunter-gatherer
and agricultural groups.
North Africa, the Central Sahel and Sudan, and the Horn
In the 7th and 8th centuries, as part of the <color=#3366CC>Arab conquests</color> which sought to spread Islamic rule, the <color=#3366CC>Rashidun</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Umayyad</color> caliphates conquered North Africa at the expense of the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> and Berber leaders such as
Kusaila and <color=#3366CC>Kahina</color>. Large numbers of Berber and <color=#3366CC>Coptic</color> people willingly converted to Islam, and followers of
<color=#3366CC>Abrahamic religions</color> ('People of the Book') were protected, though followers of Berber traditional religion were violently
oppressed. In the 8th century the Berber Revolt rocked the caliphate, and Berber dynasties took control over the
Maghreb, while the <color=#3366CC>Tulunids</color> briefly controlled Egypt.
In the 10th century, the <color=#3366CC>Fatimids</color> rose to power in modern-day Tunisia, established a rival caliphate, and <color=#3366CC>conquered</color>
<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, before expanding into the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>. In the 11th century the <color=#3366CC>Almoravids</color> conquered the Maghreb and
intervened in the Christian <color=#3366CC>reconquest of Iberia</color>. <color=#3366CC>Saladin</color>, a Fatimid <color=#3366CC>vizier</color>, usurped power in the 12th century and
established the <color=#3366CC>Ayyubid dynasty</color> which restored Egyptian prestige, while the <color=#3366CC>Almohad</color> revolution deposed the
Almoravids to the east. After Christian gains in Iberia in the 13th century, the Almohads disintegrated into the <color=#3366CC>Marinids</color>,
Zayyanids, and Hafsids in modern-day Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia respectively.
In the face of <color=#3366CC>Mongol expansion</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mamluk</color> generals <color=#3366CC>seized power</color> in Egypt and expanded into the Middle East. In the
early-16th century, the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> rapidly conquered North Africa (save for Morocco under <color=#3366CC>Saadi rule</color>) to counter
Spanish expansionism. In the following centuries, over a million Europeans are estimated to have been captured
captured and enslaved by <color=#3366CC>Barbary corsairs</color>. The Ottoman regencies became more independent during the 18th
century.
In the central Sahel around Lake Chad, the <color=#3366CC>Kanem–Bornu Empire</color> ruled from the 6th century, and projected power over
the <color=#3366CC>Hausa Kingdoms</color>. To the east during 7th century, <color=#3366CC>Makuria</color> conquered Nobatia to become the dominant power in the
region and resisted Muslim expansion. They later entered a severe decline following civil war and Arab migrations to
the Sudan and had disintegrated by the 15th century, giving rise to the <color=#3366CC>Funj Sultanate</color>. The Tunjur kingdom's collapse
in the central Sudan saw the rise of the Bagirmi, Wadai, and Darfur sultanates, which frequently raided the populations
to their south for slaves.
In the Horn of Africa, Aksum lost control of the Red Sea, and its isolation from Christendom caused Ethiopian society to
introspect and take inspiration from the <color=#3366CC>Old Testament</color>. Islamised Beja invaded the Ethiopian Highlands, forcing Aksum
to migrate south, where, according to tradition, Aksum's expansion was met by a Jewish or traditionalist queen who
destroyed the state c. 960. During the 13th century, hegemony in the Horn was contested by the Christian Zagwe, the
Muslims of Shewa, and the traditionalist Damot; the <color=#3366CC>Solomonic dynasty</color> overthrew the Zagwe to found the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>, while Shewa was replaced by Ifat. Soon after, Ethiopia conquered Damot and the Muslim states, entering into
a 'golden age'.
In the 16th century Muslims united behind <color=#3366CC>Adal</color> in <color=#3366CC>jihad</color> to reconquer the Muslim lands and occupy Ethiopia, until, with
<color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> assistance, Ethiopia counter-attacked, and its sovereignty was restored in a reduced state. The 16th and
17th centuries also saw <color=#3366CC>Oromo invasions</color> into the Horn, weakening Ethiopia further and causing the collapse of Adal,
while <color=#3366CC>Ajuran</color> on the east coast also disintegrated. Ethiopia briefly consolidated its authority in the late-17th century,
though the turn of the century saw fragmentation and gradually-increasing anarchy, which continued throughout the
18th century.
West Africa
The <color=#3366CC>Ghana Empire</color> formed in the Sahel from between the 2nd and 8th centuries, while from the 7th century the <color=#3366CC>Gao</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> ruled to its east. Almoravid capture of royal Aoudaghost led to Ghana's conversion to Islam in the 11th century,
and climatic changes led to Ghana's conquest by its vassal Sosso Empire in the 13th century. Sosso was quickly
overthrown by the <color=#3366CC>Mali Empire</color> who conquered Gao and dominated the trans-Saharan trade. The <color=#3366CC>Mossi Kingdoms</color>
were established to its south.
The 15th century saw the crumbling of the Mali Empire, with the dominant power in the region becoming the <color=#3366CC>Songhai</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> centered on <color=#3366CC>Gao</color>. Weakened by internal conflict, in 1591 Gao was conquered by Morocco, and the political
vacuum came to be filled by the Segou Empire and several other states. The once lucrative trans-Saharan trade
gradually lost its prominence to the coastal Atlantic trade with Europeans, and the following centuries saw many
droughts, famines, and epidemics.
In the forest regions of West Africa, various kingdoms and empires flourished, such as the <color=#3366CC>Yoruba</color> empires of Ife and

<color=#3366CC>Oyo</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Igbo</color> <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Nri</color>, the Edo <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Benin</color> (famous for its art), the Dagomba Kingdom of Dagbon, and
the Akan kingdoms of Bonoman and Adanse. They came into contact with the Portuguese in the 15th century which
saw the start of the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Asante Empire</color> was established in present-day Ghana. Between 1515 and
1800, 8 million Africans were exported in the Atlantic slave trade.
Central Africa
In the western Congo Basin by the 13th century there were three main confederations of states: the Seven Kingdoms,
Mpemba, and one led by Vungu. In the 14th century the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kongo</color> emerged and dominated the region, with
the Tio Kingdom to its north and Mwene Muji to its northeast. Portuguese arrival in the 15th century saw Kongo's ruler
willingly convert to Catholicism and the start of the Atlantic trade, with slaves being the most lucrative export; in the
16th century, <color=#3366CC>Afonso I</color>'s conquests produced many captives for Kongo's <color=#3366CC>monopoly</color>, and the slave trade rapidly grew to
meet demand in the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>. Over the course of the late-16th and 17th centuries, the Portuguese sought to conquer
Ndongo (allied to Matamba) in the Angolan Wars; despite fierce resistance from Queen <color=#3366CC>Nzinga</color>, and brief occupation of
Luanda by the <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color> (allied to Kongo), Portugal controlled most of Ndongo by the 1670s. The late-17th century saw
Kongo fragment between royal houses as several vassals broke away; by the time of Kongo's restoration in 1709, it
had ceased being the dominant regional power. Also during the 17th century, in the textile-producing northeast, the
Boma, Yaka, and possibly the Kuba and Pende kingdoms broke away from Mwene Muji.
In the eastern Congo Basin, farmers, fishermen, and hunters (often Pygmies) built symbiotic relations. Jan Vansina
wrote that in the southern savanna 'lords of the land' held priestly roles due to their special relationship with the spirits
of the land, and held sway over multiple villages, effectively ruling embryonic kingdoms. Accordingly, as lineages grew,
authority was opportunistically absorbed or incorporated by force. The centre of the <color=#3366CC>Luba Empire</color> is yet to undergo
archaeological research, meaning knowledge about its rise is limited; its foundation is typically dated to the 14th/15th
centuries, though scholarly estimates range from the 8th to 17th centuries. A <color=#3366CC>Lunda state</color> formed in the Nkalany Valley
(estimates range from c. 1450 to c. 1700), in the 18th century, Lunda rapidly expanded into an extensive
commonwealth across the southern savanna, using the institutions of perpetual kinship and positional succession to
incorporate peoples. Meanwhile, Luba expanded its number of tributaries, in some cases using its widely
acknowledged prestige to intervene in succession disputes and distribute ritually-powerful royal regalia related to
bulopwe (sacred kingship), in other cases using conquest.
In the northern Great Lakes, the Empire of Kitara rose around the 11th century, famed for its oral traditions. Historian
Peter Robertshaw considers its rulers (the Chwezi) to have been religious leaders who utilised networks of hill-top
shrines to project authority. Around 1500, severe droughts and famine destabilised the region, occurring again during
the early-17th and 18th centuries. Luo-speaking peoples migrated from the Upper Nile basin into modern-day Uganda,
and a Biito dynasty replaced the Chwezi in Bunyoro-Kitara. Over the following centuries, the kingdoms of
Bunyoro-Kitara, Buganda, and Rwanda struggled for hegemony among others. Throughout the 16th and 17th
centuries, Bunyoro raided states to the south such as Nkore and Rwanda. Mpororo rose and fragmented during the
18th century, while Buganda rapidly expanded at the expense of Bunyoro to become the major power in the region.
Eastern and Southern Africa
The East African interior was inhabited by pastoralist Cushitic and <color=#3366CC>Nilotic</color> speakers, along with Bantu speakers who
continued to expand and adapt to their lands while absorbing the former two; the 17th century saw the establishment of
tributary systems that stabilised the region. On the <color=#3366CC>Swahili coast</color> the <color=#3366CC>Swahili city-states</color> thrived off of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color>
<color=#3366CC>trade</color> and gradually Islamized, giving rise to the <color=#3366CC>Kilwa Sultanate</color> from the 10th century. In the 15th century, trade routes
for Zimbabwean gold shifted north, weakening Kilwa. The Portuguese arrived at the coast soon after and exploited
divisions between coastal city-states to gain control over them while utilising a powerful navy. In the 17th and 18th
centuries, Lamu-Swahili cities rebelled against the Portuguese and allied the <color=#3366CC>Omani Empire</color> which supplanted
Portuguese rule.
Madagascar was settled by <color=#3366CC>Austronesian peoples</color> between the 5th and 7th centuries, as societies organized at the
behest of hasina and competed over with one another over the island's estuaries and bridgeheads. From around the
15th century, southern Madagascar became integrated into global trade; the Sakalava Empire rose to dominate
west-coastal trade, accompanied by numerous other states, and the island saw several failed European colonial
ventures.
In Southern Africa, an early kingdom was Mapungubwe, which collapsed c. 1300 as <color=#3366CC>Great Zimbabwe</color>, with its
monumental dry-stone walls, rose to become the region's main political and economic centre. Following shifting trade
routes north to the <color=#3366CC>Zambezi</color> and unclear circumstances, Great Zimbabwe entered into decline and was succeeded by
the <color=#3366CC>Mutapa Empire</color> and Kingdom of Butua in the 15th century. Mutapa was briefly vassalised by the Portuguese in the
17th century, the latter half of which saw widespread famine and disease, until Changamire Dombo revolted in the
1680s, conquered Butua to found the Rozvi Empire, and expelled all Portuguese from the Zimbabwean plateau. <color=#3366CC>Maravi</color>
around <color=#3366CC>Lake Malawi</color> expanded in the 17th century, but the collapse of its succession system in the 18th century
precipitated its disintegration.
By the late-1st millennium CE, Bantu-speaking farmers populated most of Southern Africa's cultivable savannas,
reaching southwards to the Kei River; they traded goods such as livestock, grain, and metal tools between communities
and with hunter-gatherers. Around the 11th century, more agriculturists—who likely brought with them ancestral Nguni
and Sotho-Tswana languages—migrated across the <color=#3366CC>Limpopo River</color> and came to dominate the earlier farmers both
politically and culturally, organising into loosely-defined chiefdoms that held dynamic alliance networks. Further south,
the Dutch began colonizing the <color=#3366CC>western Cape</color> in the 17th century, and Britain seized control of the <color=#3366CC>Dutch Cape Colony</color>
around the turn of the 19th century. In the late-18th century, the interplay of pre-existing trends of political centralization
with the effects of international trade, environmental instability, and European colonisation set the <color=#3366CC>Mfecane</color> ("Crushing")
in motion, as various African states were founded.
By the turn of the 19th century, many of Africa's economic and political structures were unstable and brittle as a result
of long-term effects of the slave trade. In Egypt <color=#3366CC>Muhammad Ali</color> led a national movement to seize power from Ottoman
suzerainty, instituting sweeping reforms and greatly strengthening Egyptian power by militaristic expansion. Meanwhile,
in West Africa the <color=#3366CC>Fula jihads</color>, which had been gaining momentum throughout the 18th century, culminated in the
establishment of the expansive <color=#3366CC>Sokoto</color> and Hamdullahi caliphates. In the Horn, Ethiopia underwent reforms, seeking to
revive the imperial state, something that was later achieved by Menelik II's conquests. In Southern Africa the <color=#3366CC>Mfecane</color>
propelled large long-distance migrations that caused widespread disruption across the vast region, while several <color=#3366CC>Boer</color>
<color=#3366CC>republics</color> were founded. European campaigns to abolish the Atlantic slave trade led to supply refocusing on internal
markets and saw the rapid growth of the Indian Ocean slave trade. Across the continent many rulers attempted reforms
and indigenous forms of 'modernisation', however these efforts were consistently undermined by European traders and
missionaries as the tide of European encroachment rose.
For 400 years, European nations had mainly limited their involvement to trading stations on the African coast, with few
daring to venture inland. The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> in Europe produced several technological innovations which assisted
them in overcoming this 400-year pattern. One was the development of repeating rifles, which were easier and quicker
to load than <color=#3366CC>muskets</color>. <color=#3366CC>Artillery</color> was being used increasingly. In 1885, <color=#3366CC>Hiram Maxim</color> developed the maxim gun, the
model of the modern-day <color=#3366CC>machine gun</color>. European states kept these weapons largely among themselves by refusing to
sell these weapons to African leaders. African germs took numerous European lives and deterred <color=#3366CC>permanent</color>

<color=#3366CC>settlements</color>. Diseases such as <color=#3366CC>yellow fever</color>, <color=#3366CC>sleeping sickness</color>, yaws, and <color=#3366CC>leprosy</color> made Africa a very inhospitable
place for Europeans. The deadliest disease was <color=#3366CC>malaria</color>, endemic throughout Tropical Africa. In 1854, the discovery of
<color=#3366CC>quinine</color> and other medical innovations helped to make conquest and colonisation in Africa possible.
There were strong motives for the conquest of Africa. Raw materials were needed for European factories, and free
trade was championed to prevent Africans from regulating their economies. Prestige and imperial rivalries were at play.
Acquiring African colonies would show rivals that a nation was powerful and significant. These contextual factors forged
the <color=#3366CC>Scramble for Africa</color>; during the late-19th and early-20th centuries the European powers partitioned and conquered
almost all of Africa despite fierce resistance (only Ethiopia and <color=#3366CC>Liberia</color> remained independent). Traditional leaders were
incorporated into the colonial regimes as a form of indirect rule to extract human and natural resources and curb
organized resistance. Colonial borders were drawn unilaterally by the Europeans, often cutting across bonds of kinship,
language, culture, and established routes, and sometimes incorporating groups who previously had little in common.
The threat to trade routes was mitigated by poor policing and African entrepreneurs (viewed as smugglers) who
exploited the differing tax and legal schemes. The first few decades of European colonialism saw intense violence,
disorder, and atrocities, such as that of the <color=#3366CC>Congo Free State</color>, <color=#3366CC>German South West Africa</color>, and French Algeria, with the
late colonial period relatively peaceful in comparison. Colonial rule had wide-reaching effects on African societies, such
as the spread of Christianity as part of the 'civilising mission'. African culture was strongly denigrated and persecuted,
as pervasive racial discrimination deepened the scars of humiliation.
Independence struggles
Imperial rule by Europeans continued until after the conclusion of <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, when almost all remaining colonial
territories gradually obtained formal independence. <color=#3366CC>Independence movements in Africa</color> gained momentum following
World War II, which left the major European powers weakened. In 1951, Libya, a former Italian colony, gained
independence. In 1956, Tunisia and Morocco won their independence from France. Ghana followed suit in 1957),
becoming the first of the sub-Saharan colonies to be granted independence. Over the next decade, waves of
decolonisation took place across the continent, culminating in the 1960 Year of Africa and the establishment of the
<color=#3366CC>Organisation of African Unity</color> in 1963.
Portugal's overseas presence in sub-Saharan Africa (most notably in Angola, Cape Verde, Mozambique,
Guinea-Bissau, and São Tomé and Príncipe) lasted from the 16th century to 1975, after the <color=#3366CC>Estado Novo</color> regime was
overthrown in <color=#3366CC>a military coup in Lisbon</color>. <color=#3366CC>Rhodesia</color> unilaterally declared independence from the United Kingdom in 1965,
under the white minority government of <color=#3366CC>Ian Smith</color> but was not internationally recognised as an independent state (as
<color=#3366CC>Zimbabwe</color>) until 1980, when black nationalists gained power after a <color=#3366CC>bitter guerrilla war</color>. Although South Africa was one
of the first African countries to gain independence, the state remained under the control of the country's white minority,
initially through qualified voting rights and from 1956 by a system of <color=#3366CC>racial segregation</color> known as <color=#3366CC>apartheid</color>, until 1994.
Post-colonial Africa
As of 2025, Africa contains 54 sovereign countries. Since independence, African states have frequently been
hampered by instability, corruption, violence, and authoritarianism. The vast majority of African states are republics that
operate under some form of the <color=#3366CC>presidential system</color> of rule. However, few of them have been able to sustain
democratic governments on a permanent basis—per the criteria laid out by Lührmann et al. (2018), only <color=#3366CC>Botswana</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Mauritius</color> have been consistently democratic for the entirety of their post-colonial history. Most African countries have
experienced several coups or periods of <color=#3366CC>military dictatorship</color>. Between 1990 and 2018, though, the continent as a
whole has trended towards more democratic governance.
Upon independence an overwhelming majority of Africans lived in extreme poverty. The continent suffered from the
lack of infrastructural or industrial development under colonial rule, along with political instability. With limited financial
resources or access to global markets, relatively stable countries such as <color=#3366CC>Kenya</color> still experienced only very slow
economic development. Only a handful of countries succeeded in obtaining rapid economic growth prior to 1990.
Exceptions include Libya and Equatorial Guinea, both of which possess large oil reserves.
Instability after decolonisation resulted primarily from marginalisation of ethnic groups, and corruption. In pursuit of
personal political gain, many leaders deliberately promoted ethnic conflicts, some of which had originated during the
colonial period, such as from the grouping of multiple unrelated ethnic groups into a single colony, the splitting of a
distinct ethnic group between multiple colonies, or existing conflicts being exacerbated by colonial rule (for instance, the
preferential treatment given to ethnic Hutus over <color=#3366CC>Tutsis</color> in Rwanda during German and Belgian rule).
Faced with increasingly frequent and severe violence, military rule was widely accepted by the population of many
countries as means to maintain order, and during the 1970s and 1980s a majority of African countries were controlled
by military dictatorships. Territorial disputes between nations and rebellions by groups seeking independence were also
common in independent African states. The most devastating of these was the <color=#3366CC>Nigerian Civil War</color>, fought between
government forces and an <color=#3366CC>Igbo</color> <color=#3366CC>separatist republic</color>, which resulted in a famine that killed 1–2 million people. Two civil
wars in Sudan, <color=#3366CC>the first</color> lasting from 1955 to 1972 and <color=#3366CC>the second</color> from 1983 to 2005, collectively killed around 3 million.
Both were fought primarily on ethnic and religious lines.
<color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> conflicts between the United States and the Soviet Union also contributed to instability. Both the Soviet Union
and the United States offered considerable incentives to political and military leaders who aligned themselves with the
superpowers' foreign policy. As an example, during the <color=#3366CC>Angolan Civil War</color>, the Soviet and Cuban aligned <color=#3366CC>MPLA</color> and the
American aligned UNITA received the vast majority of their military and political support from these countries. Many
African countries became highly dependent on foreign aid. The sudden loss of both Soviet and American aid at the end
of the Cold War and <color=#3366CC>fall of the USSR</color> resulted in severe economic and political turmoil in the countries most dependent
on foreign support.
There was a <color=#3366CC>major famine in Ethiopia</color> between 1983 and 1985, killing up to 1.2 million people, which most historians
attribute primarily to the forced relocation of farmworkers and seizure of grain by the communist <color=#3366CC>Derg</color> government,
further exacerbated by the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Civil War</color>. In 1994 a <color=#3366CC>genocide in Rwanda</color> resulted in up to 800,000 deaths, added
to a severe refugee crisis and fuelled the rise of militia groups in neighbouring countries. This contributed to the
outbreak of the <color=#3366CC>first</color> and <color=#3366CC>second</color> Congo Wars, which were the most devastating military conflicts in modern Africa, with
up to 5.5 million deaths, making it by far the deadliest conflict in modern African history and one of the costliest wars in
human history. In 2025 it is estimated 20% of Africans face hunger in 2025, compared to 6% of Asia, 5% in Latin
America and the Caribbean, 8% in Oceania, and less than 2.5% in North America and Europe.
Various conflicts between various insurgent groups and governments continue. From 2003-2020 a <color=#3366CC>conflict in Darfur</color>
resulted in around 300,000 deaths. The <color=#3366CC>Boko Haram insurgency</color> in Sub-Saharan Africa has killed around 350,000
people since 2009. The <color=#3366CC>Tigray war</color> from 2020 to 2022 killed an estimated 300,000–500,000 people, primarily due to
famine. Overall, violence across Africa has greatly declined in the 21st century, with the end of civil wars in Angola,

<color=#3366CC>Sierra Leone</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> in 2002, <color=#3366CC>Liberia</color> in 2003, and <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Burundi</color> in 2005. The Second Congo War, which
involved 9 countries and several insurgent groups, ended in 2003. This decline in violence coincided with many
countries abandoning communist-style command economies and opening up for market reforms, which over the course
of the 1990s and 2000s promoted the establishment of permanent, peaceful trade between neighbouring countries.
Improved stability and economic reforms have led to a great increase in foreign investment into many nations, mainly
from China, which further spurred economic growth. Between 2000 and 2014, annual GDP growth in sub-Saharan
Africa averaged 5%, doubling its total GDP from $811 billion to $1.63 trillion (constant 2015 <color=#3366CC>USD</color>). North Africa
experienced comparable growth rates. A significant part of this growth can also be attributed to the facilitated diffusion
of information technologies and specifically the mobile telephone. While several individual countries have maintained
high growth rates, since 2014 overall growth has considerably slowed, primarily as a result of falling commodity prices,
continued lack of industrialisation, and epidemics such as <color=#3366CC>Ebola</color> and COVID-19.
Geography
Africa is the largest of the three great southward projections from the largest landmass of the Earth. Separated from
Europe by the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>, it is joined to Asia at its northeast extremity by the <color=#3366CC>Isthmus of Suez</color> (transected by
the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color>), 163 km wide. Geopolitically, Egypt's <color=#3366CC>Sinai Peninsula</color> east of the Suez Canal is often considered part
of Africa as well.
The coastline is 26000 km long, and the absence of deep indentations of the shore is illustrated by the fact that Europe,
which covers only 10400000 km2 – about a third of the surface of Africa – has a coastline of 32000 km. From the most
northerly point, Ras ben Sakka in Tunisia (37°21' N), to the most southerly point, <color=#3366CC>Cape Agulhas</color> in South Africa
(34°51'15" S), is a distance of approximately 8,000 km. Cape Verde, 17°33'22" W, the westernmost point, is a distance
of approximately 7400 km to Ras Hafun, 51°27'52" E, the most easterly projection that neighbours Cape Guardafui, the
tip of the Horn of Africa.
The largest country is Algeria and smallest is <color=#3366CC>Seychelles</color>, an <color=#3366CC>archipelago</color> off the east coast. The smallest nation on the
continental mainland is <color=#3366CC>The Gambia</color>.
African plate
Climate
The climate of Africa ranges from <color=#3366CC>tropical</color> to <color=#3366CC>subarctic</color> on its highest peaks. Its northern half is primarily <color=#3366CC>desert</color> or arid,
while its central and southern areas contain both <color=#3366CC>savanna</color> plains and dense <color=#3366CC>jungle</color> (<color=#3366CC>rainforest</color>) regions. In between,
there is a convergence, where vegetation patterns such as <color=#3366CC>sahel</color> and <color=#3366CC>steppe</color> dominate. Africa is the hottest continent
on Earth, and 60% of the land surface consists of drylands and deserts. The record for the highest-ever recorded
temperature, in <color=#3366CC>Libya</color> in 1922 (58 C), was discredited in 2013.
Climate change
Ecology and biodiversity
Africa has over 3,000 <color=#3366CC>protected areas</color>, with 198 marine protected areas, 50 biosphere reserves, and 80 wetlands
reserves. Significant habitat destruction, increases in human population, and poaching are reducing the biological
diversity and <color=#3366CC>arable land</color>. Human encroachment, civil unrest and the introduction of non-native species threaten
biodiversity. This has been exacerbated by administrative problems, inadequate personnel and funding problems.
<color=#3366CC>Deforestation</color> is affecting Africa at twice the world rate, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. The
deforestation rate of 4.08 million hectares in 2000–2015 declined to 3.45 million ha per year in 2015–2025. According
to the University of Pennsylvania African Studies Center, 31% of pasture lands and 19% of forests and woodlands are
classified as degraded, and the deforestation rate is twice the average for the rest of the world. Some sources claim
that approximately 90% of the original, virgin forests in West Africa have been destroyed. Over 90% of <color=#3366CC>Madagascar</color>'s
original forests have been destroyed since the arrival of humans 2,000 years ago. About 65% of agricultural land
suffers from soil degradation.
Fauna
Africa boasts perhaps the world's largest combination of density and "range of freedom" of wild animal populations and
diversity, with wild populations of large carnivores (such as <color=#3366CC>lions</color>, <color=#3366CC>hyenas</color>, and <color=#3366CC>cheetahs</color>) and herbivores (such as

<color=#3366CC>buffalo</color>, <color=#3366CC>elephants</color>, <color=#3366CC>camels</color>, and <color=#3366CC>giraffes</color>) ranging freely on primarily open non-private plains. It is also home to a variety
of "jungle" animals including snakes and primates and aquatic life such as crocodiles and amphibians. Africa has the
largest number of <color=#3366CC>megafauna</color> species, as it was least affected by the <color=#3366CC>extinction of the Pleistocene megafauna</color>.
Environmental issues
Politics
African Union
The <color=#3366CC>African Union</color> (AU) is a continental union consisting of 55 member states. The union was formed with <color=#3366CC>Addis Ababa</color>
as its headquarters in 2001 as a successor to the <color=#3366CC>Organisation of African Unity</color>. The Pan-African Parliament (PAP) is
located in Midrand, South Africa.
The African Union, not to be confused with the AU Commission, is formed by the Constitutive Act of the African Union,
which aims to transform the African Economic Community, a federated commonwealth, into a state under established
international conventions. The Assembly of the African Union consists of legislative, judicial and executive organs. It is
led by the African Union president and head of state, who is also the president of PAP. The president is elected by
PAP. The powers and authority of the president of the Assembly derive from the Constitutive Act and the Protocol of
the Pan-African Parliament, as well as the inheritance of presidential authority stipulated by African treaties and by
international treaties. The government consists of all-union, regional, state, and municipal authorities, as well as
hundreds of institutions, that together manage the day-to-day affairs of the institution.
Extensive human rights abuses still occur in several parts of Africa, often under the oversight of the state. Most of such
violations occur for political reasons, often as a side effect of civil war. Countries where major human rights violations
have been reported in recent times include the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Sudan,
Zimbabwe, and Ivory Coast.

Economy
Although it has abundant natural resources, Africa remains the world's poorest and <color=#3366CC>least-developed</color> continent (other
than Antarctica), the result of a variety of causes that may include corrupt governments that have often committed
serious human rights violations, failed central planning, high levels of illiteracy, low self-esteem, lack of access to
foreign capital, legacies of colonialism, the slave trade, the Cold War, and frequent tribal and military conflict (ranging
from guerrilla warfare to genocide). The continent's total nominal GDP remains behind that of several individual
countries, including the United States, China, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, India and France. According to the
United Nations' Human Development Report in 2003, the bottom 24 ranked nations (151st to 175th) were all African.
Poverty, illiteracy, malnutrition, inadequate <color=#3366CC>water supply and sanitation</color>, and poor health affect a large proportion of the
people. A 2008 <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> estimates 81% of the sub-Saharan African population were living on less than $2.50 (PPP)
per day in 2005, compared with 86% for India. Sub-Saharan Africa is the least successful region of the world in
reducing poverty; some 50% of the population living in poverty in 1981 (200 million people), a figure that rose to 58% in
1996 before dropping to 50% in 2005 (380 million people). The average poor person in sub-Saharan Africa is estimated
to live on only 70 cents per day and was poorer in 2003 than in 1973, indicating increasing poverty in some areas.
Some of it is attributed to unsuccessful economic liberalisation programmes spearheaded by foreign companies and
governments, but other studies cite bad domestic government policies more than external factors.
The last debt crisis in 2005 was resolved with help from the heavily indebted poor countries scheme, which resulted in
some positive and negative effects on the economy in Africa. About 10 years after the 2005 debt crisis in sub-Saharan
Africa was resolved, Zambia fell back into debt. A small reason was due to the fall in copper prices in 2011, but the
bigger reason was that a large amount of the money Zambia borrowed was wasted or pocketed by the elite.
From 1995 to 2005, Africa's rate of economic growth increased, averaging 5% in 2005. Some countries experienced
still higher growth rates, notably Angola, Sudan and Equatorial Guinea, all of which had increased oil production.
The following table shows the projected nominal GDP and GDP per capita (at <color=#3366CC>purchasing power parity</color>) in 2026 by the
<color=#3366CC>IMF</color>.
The continent is believed to hold 90% of the world's <color=#3366CC>cobalt</color>, 90% of its <color=#3366CC>platinum</color>, 50% of its gold, 98% of its <color=#3366CC>chromium</color>,

70% of its <color=#3366CC>tantalite</color>, 64% of its <color=#3366CC>manganese</color> and one-third of its <color=#3366CC>uranium</color>. The DRC has 70% of the world's <color=#3366CC>coltan</color>, a
mineral used in the production of tantalum capacitors for electronic devices such as cell phones. The DRC also has
more than 30% of the world's diamond reserves. Guinea is the world's largest exporter of <color=#3366CC>bauxite</color>. As the growth in
Africa has been driven mainly by services and not manufacturing or agriculture, it has been growth without jobs and
without reduction in poverty levels. In fact, the food security crisis of 2008 (which took place following the <color=#3366CC>global</color>
<color=#3366CC>financial crisis</color>) pushed 100 million people into food insecurity. In 2024 nearly 307 million people were undernourished
(46% of the global total), an increase of 10 million people since 2023 and 34 million from 2022.
China has built increasingly stronger ties with African nations and is Africa's largest trading partner. In 2007, Chinese
companies invested a total of US$1 billion in Africa.
A <color=#3366CC>Harvard University</color> study led by professor Calestous Juma shows that Africa could feed itself by making the transition
from importer to self-sufficiency. "African agriculture is at the crossroads; we have come to the end of a century of
policies that favoured Africa's export of raw materials and importation of food. Africa is starting to focus on agricultural
innovation as its new engine for regional trade and prosperity."
Energy
Infrastructure
Water resources
Water development and management are complex due to the multiplicity of trans-boundary water resources (rivers,
lakes and aquifers). Around 75% of sub-Saharan Africa falls within 53 international river basin catchments that traverse
multiple borders. This particular constraint can also be converted into an opportunity if the potential for trans-boundary
cooperation is harnessed in the development of the area's water resources. A multi-sectoral analysis of the <color=#3366CC>Zambezi</color>
River, for example, shows that <color=#3366CC>riparian</color> cooperation could lead to a 23% increase in firm energy production without any
additional investments. Several institutional and legal frameworks for transboundary cooperation exist, such as the
Zambezi River Authority, the <color=#3366CC>Southern African Development Community</color> protocol, Volta River Authority and the Nile
Basin Commission. However, additional efforts are required to further develop political will as well as the financial
capacities and institutional frameworks needed for multilateral cooperative actions and optimal solutions for all
riparians.
Demographics
Africa is considered by anthropologists to be the most genetically diverse continent as a result of being the longest
inhabited. The population has rapidly increased over the last 40 years and is consequently relatively young. In some
states, more than half the population is under 25 years of age. The population increased from 229 million in 1950 to
630 million in 1990. As of, the population is estimated at. Africa's total population surpassing other continents is fairly
recent; the population surpassed Europe in the 1990s, while the Americas was overtaken sometime around 2000. This
increase in number of babies born in Africa compared to the rest of the world is expected to reach approximately 37%
in the year 2050; while in 1990 sub-Saharan Africa accounted for only 16% of the world's births.
The total fertility rate (children per woman) for sub-Saharan Africa is 4.7 as of 2018, the highest in the world. All
countries in sub-Saharan Africa had rates above replacement level in 2019 and accounted for 27.1% of global live
births. In 2021, sub-Saharan Africa accounted for 29% of global births.
Speakers of <color=#3366CC>Bantu languages</color> (part of the <color=#3366CC>Niger–Congo</color> family) are the majority in southern, central and southeast
Africa. The Bantu-speaking peoples from the Sahel progressively expanded over most of sub-Saharan Africa. But there
are also several <color=#3366CC>Nilotic</color> groups in South Sudan and East Africa, the mixed Swahili people on the <color=#3366CC>Swahili coast</color>, and a
few remaining indigenous Khoisan and Pygmy peoples in Southern and Central Africa, respectively. Bantu speakers
predominate in Gabon and Equatorial Guinea and are found in parts of southern Cameroon. In the <color=#3366CC>Kalahari Desert</color> the
distinct people known as the Bushmen (also "<color=#3366CC>San</color>", closely related to but distinct from <color=#3366CC>Khoekhoe</color>) have long been
present. The San are physically distinct from other Africans and are the indigenous people of southern Africa. Pygmies
are the pre-Bantu indigenous peoples of Central Africa.
The peoples of West Africa primarily speak Niger–Congo languages, belonging mostly to its non-Bantu branches,

though some <color=#3366CC>Nilo-Saharan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Afroasiatic</color> speaking groups are also found. The Niger–Congo-speaking <color=#3366CC>Yoruba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Igbo</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Fulani</color>, <color=#3366CC>Akan</color>, and Wolof ethnic groups are the largest and most influential. In the central Sahara, Mandinka or Mande
groups are most significant. Chadic-speaking groups, including the <color=#3366CC>Hausa</color>, are found in more northerly parts of the
region nearest to the Sahara. Nilo-Saharan communities such as the Songhai, Kanuri, and Zarma are found in eastern
West Africa.
The peoples of North Africa consist of three main indigenous groups: <color=#3366CC>Berbers</color> in the northwest, Egyptians in the
northeast, and Nilo-Saharan-speaking peoples in the east. The Arabs who arrived in the 7th century introduced the
Arabic language and Islam to North Africa. The Semitic <color=#3366CC>Phoenicians</color> (who founded <color=#3366CC>Carthage</color>) and <color=#3366CC>Hyksos</color>, the
Indo-Iranian <color=#3366CC>Alans</color>, the Indo-European <color=#3366CC>Greeks</color>, Romans, and <color=#3366CC>Vandals</color> settled in North Africa as well. Significant Berber
communities remain within Morocco and Algeria in the 21st century, while, Berber speakers are also present in some
regions of Tunisia and Libya. The Berber-speaking <color=#3366CC>Tuareg</color> and other often nomadic peoples are the principal
inhabitants of the Saharan interior of North Africa. In Mauritania, there is a small nearly extinct Berber community in the
north and Niger–Congo-speaking peoples in the south, though in both regions Arabic and Arab culture predominates.
In Sudan, although Arabic and Arab culture predominate, it is mostly inhabited by groups that originally spoke
Nilo-Saharan, such as the Nubians, Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa, who, over the centuries, have variously intermixed with
migrants from the Arabian peninsula. Small communities of Afroasiatic-speaking Beja nomads are found in Egypt and
Sudan.
In the Horn of Africa, some Ethiopian and Eritrean groups (like the <color=#3366CC>Amhara</color> and Tigrayans, collectively known as
<color=#3366CC>Habesha</color>) speak languages from the <color=#3366CC>Semitic</color> branch of the Afroasiatic language family, while the <color=#3366CC>Oromo</color> and Somali
speak languages from the Cushitic branch of Afroasiatic.
Prior to the decolonisation movements of the post-World War II era, Europeans were represented in every part of
Africa. Decolonization during the 1960s and 1970s often resulted in the mass emigration of white settlers—especially
from Algeria and Morocco (1.6 million pieds-noirs in North Africa), Kenya, Congo, Rhodesia, Mozambique and Angola.
Between 1975 and 1977, over a million colonials returned to Portugal alone. Nevertheless, white Africans remain an
important minority in many African states, particularly Zimbabwe, Namibia, Réunion, and South Africa. The country with
the largest white African population is South Africa. Dutch and British diasporas represent the largest communities of
European ancestry on the continent.
European colonisation brought sizable groups of Asians, particularly South Asians, to British colonies. Large <color=#3366CC>Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>communities</color> are found in South Africa, and smaller ones are present in Kenya, Tanzania, and some other southern
and southeast African countries. The large Indian community in Uganda was expelled by <color=#3366CC>Idi Amin</color> in 1972, though
many have since returned. The islands in the Indian Ocean are populated primarily by people of Asian origin, often
mixed with Africans and Europeans. The Malagasy peoples of Madagascar are an <color=#3366CC>Austronesian people</color>, but those
along the coast are generally mixed with Bantu, Arab, Indian and European origins. Malay and Indian ancestries are
components in Cape Coloureds (people with origins in two or more races and continents). During the 20th century,
small but economically important communities of Lebanese have developed in West and East Africa.
